rv.q: The conclusion of this rich entertainment isn’t what you expect
Leguizamo's boisterous, chalk-covered persona and Peter Sellers-esque gift for mimicry more than make up for any lack of historiographical subtlety
Leguizamo has always been a master of voices and physicality, and in Latin History for Morons he puts those skills to use in service of a genuinely educational and deeply personal show.
His takes on everyone from Sigmund Freud to Andrew Jackson are righteously funny, if bordering on the obscene, and there are some pointed messages about immigration issues.

But for the first time in his solo Broadway career, which began with “Freak” in 1998 and reached peaks with “Sexaholix” in 2001 and “Ghetto Klown” in 2011, Mr. Leguizamo is unable to make a convincing cartoon of himself.
But he has now donned a professorial three-piece suit, armed himself with chalk and factoids, and put his respectability on the line.
Though amusing at first, these sequences eventually start to flag.
As a solo performer — and I'm counting all Americans — he ranks among the very best.

Leguizamo needs to make room on his shelf of accomplishments because Latin History For Morons is a powerful, and powerfully funny lecture that should once again garner awards for its creator and professor.
With Latin History for Morons, Leguizamo isn’t merely teaching us what we’ve never been taught.
The man knows his audience, and his Latin lesson is a treat.
He is funny, charming, has a limitless range of voices to portray his multiple characters, and above all, injects his material with a Thanksgiving-size portion of humanity.

Even if you aren't already among the legions of whooping Leguizamo fans who have turned up at both shows I attended off and on Broadway, you are likely to be among the converted by the time you leave.
It's a tough balancing act, one which Leguizamo manages with the skill of the most experienced tightrope walker.
He can rumba across the stage, make ridiculous faces, and concoct the most Martian-sounding French accent and it never feels like too much.
“Latin History for Morons” is the most fun

“The show is fast-paced, funny, foul-mouthed, insightful and, on the down side, occasionally cringe-worthy...Amid the commentary Leguizamo slips in and out of Spanish, busts out dance moves and apes accents of friends, family, and famous figures. Leguizamo is a terrific mimic..Still, doing voices of a deaf relative and scientist Stephen Hawking...
It's entertaining but its running time...could lead to restlessness for those who are not major fans.
Morons is entertaining and damning all at once

Although one can appreciate the sincerity behind Leguizamo’s emphasis on his family, his long-winded attempt to dramatize conversations with his son, wife and daughter falls flat and weighs down the rest of the show, in which he interacts directly with the audience with flair, fervor and ease.
Leguizamo's punch lines, potent and hilarious as they may be, have a serious undercurrent that propels director Tony Taccone's production.
Directed by Tony Taccone, hilarious, important, and upsetting are some of the most poignant terms to describe John Leguizamo’s Latin History For Morons.

"Unapologetic, of-the-moment, matured and funny...Leguizamo delivers his signature brand of humor, self-deprecation with a newfound responsibility to bring political awareness to the mistreatment of Latino immigrants by the current administration...Definitely worth seeing.
With his singular voice, he teaches some good lessons in “Latin History for Morons”, serving low-brow comedy alongside meaningful, and necessary, social commentary.

"It’s his usual combination of dead-on impressions, penetrating observations, juvenile humor and unabashed sentimentality...With a chalkboard at center stage to visualize the teaching concept (Tony Taccone’s direction is happily haphazard), Leguizamo blends his one-of-a-kind riffing, caricature and vocal impersonation into an offbeat lecture...
It truly is a lesson not only he or his

They are unnecessary and undercut his whole argument, all for the sake of cheap laughs.

He educates his son, himself, and the audience on unsung major figures in American history through the physical comedy that has made him one of the most celebrated comedians of the last thirty years and displays an unsparing political fierceness that feels necessary in comedy right now.

cn.t: Leguizamo delivers an energetic, hilarious history lesson that's politically urgent and surprisingly educational, though some find it overstuffed and overlong. His signature comedic skills shine in this personal, provocative solo show.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
